reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / NCCN & genetics references
clinicalPearls: Caused by germline variants in SMAD4 or BMPR1A, disrupting the TGF-beta/BMP signalling pathway, inherited autosomal dominantly with a significant de novo rate
The term juvenile refers to the histological type of hamartomatous polyp rather than the age of onset, though presentation is often in childhood or young adulthood
Multiple juvenile polyps develop throughout the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly in the colon and rectum but also in the stomach and small bowel
Common presenting features include rectal bleeding, iron-deficiency anaemia, and, with large polyps, intussusception, prolapse, or protein-losing enteropathy
Confers an increased lifetime risk of colorectal cancer and, especially with gastric involvement, gastric cancer, warranting endoscopic surveillance and polypectomy
SMAD4 variants are associated with a combined phenotype overlapping hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, so carriers should be screened for arteriovenous malformations
Surveillance involves periodic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and colonoscopy with polyp clearance, and colectomy or gastrectomy may be needed for uncontrollable polyp burden or cancer
A negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis given frequent de novo variants, so isolated cases with multiple juvenile polyps warrant genetic evaluation
reference.pathophysiology: SMAD4 and BMPR1A are components of the TGF-beta/BMP signalling pathway, which restrains proliferation and promotes differentiation of gastrointestinal epithelial and stromal cells. Loss of function disrupts this growth-suppressing signalling, producing the characteristic hamartomatous juvenile polyps and creating a field of mucosa predisposed to dysplastic and malignant change. SMAD4 additionally regulates vascular integrity, which explains the overlap of SMAD4-related juvenile polyposis with hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and its arteriovenous malformations.
additionalDifferentials: Cowden syndrome and other PTEN hamartoma tumour syndromes
Solitary sporadic juvenile polyp (not a syndrome)
Other mixed or hamartomatous polyposis syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Germline SMAD4 and BMPR1A sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis with genetic counselling
Colonoscopy and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with polypectomy for surveillance
Full blood count and iron studies to assess chronic gastrointestinal blood loss
Screening for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia features (including pulmonary and cerebral arteriovenous malformations) in SMAD4 carriers
redFlags: Significant or recurrent gastrointestinal bleeding with anaemia
Intussusception, rectal prolapse, or protein-losing enteropathy from heavy polyp burden
Endoscopic or histological features of dysplasia or malignancy
Complications of arteriovenous malformations in SMAD4-related disease
reference.prognosis: With regular endoscopic surveillance and polyp clearance, the risk of gastrointestinal cancer can be reduced and outcomes are favourable, though heavy polyp burden may ultimately require surgical resection. In SMAD4 carriers, prognosis also depends on identifying and managing arteriovenous malformations.
pitfalls: Regarding a juvenile polyp as invariably benign and failing to recognise the polyposis syndrome and its cancer risk
Omitting upper gastrointestinal surveillance and missing gastric polyps or cancer
Not screening SMAD4 carriers for hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and dangerous arteriovenous malformations
Assuming a negative family history excludes the diagnosis despite common de novo variants
